item.title: Pentagon quietly prepares for $400 billion cut to Trump's military budget
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Pentagon is quietly preparing for a $400 billion cut to President Donald Trump’s military budget, as officials realize the president’s record-breaking request is effectively dead. The administration has pushed Congress for a supersized $1.5 trillion investment in the military — the largest in history. The money would overhaul weapons stockpiles and realize Trump’s dreams for everything from a sprawling missile shield to a fleet of nuclear-powered battleships . But the Pentagon and congressional spending committees are drafting a smaller $1.1 trillion defense budget, according to a defense industry official, two former officials and one other person familiar with the matter. The planning — which runs contrary to what administration officials are saying publicly — is a clear indication of the political headwinds facing Republicans after the midterm elections. “The Pentagon can’t admit this,” said one of the people who, like the others, was granted anonymity to speak about internal discussions. The administration has hinged its unprecedented defense budget on a party-line process called reconciliation. This would allow Republican lawmakers to add $350 billion to a $1.15 trillion defense base budget, despite objections from Democrats. Now, Pentagon planners are evaluating what defense programs they will be forced to prioritize in the face of reduced funding, the people said. “None of them expect anywhere close to 1.5 trillion,” one of the former officials said. “They are absolutely developing plans [for less] and that is much more the expectation than anything close to 1.5 trillion.” The White House referred questions to the Pentagon, which did not respond to a request for comment. The cuts could scramble the Defense Department’s efforts to procure new weapons platforms, enter into new agreements with the defense industry or even continue existing programs. It could also affect how quickly the U.S. can rebuild weapons stockpiles severely depleted by the Iran war. The Pentagon’s latest estimates show at least $47 billion in costs associated with the conflict, with the lion’s share of that bill, $29 billion, stemming from critical munitions replacements. Trump administration officials have not offered any alternatives — at least not publicly. Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought insisted this month that “we’re not planning on failure.” The administration has not developed alternatives to fund critical Pentagon programs if Congress doesn’t back the White House’s plan, he said. But GOP infighting in both chambers has already imperiled the odds of passing even one piece of the $1.5 trillion total. Top Senate Republicans have warned they don’t have enough votes to pass a party-line spending package. And House Republicans have threatened to withhold their votes over the administration’s handling of foreign policy and a reluctance to devote more money to the military. "Republicans are increasingly angry at the administration on the defense front,” said the former official. It’s “unlikely that anything drastic, a $1.5 trillion budget, would happen.” Lawmakers will return to Washington next month with fewer than five legislative weeks to accomplish a wide range of objectives before the year’s end. If Democrats win control over one or both chambers next week, the GOP will have less than two months to push their priorities through. item.title: Pope Leo casts historic U.S. vote after years of requesting both parties' primary ballots
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide America's future as the Trump era slowly comes to an end. The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections , citing his long-standing belief in civic participation. Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” and has done so “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said. The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. Leo lived in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years. “The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added. Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship, and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections. This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they’re also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin’s retirement. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot but he has campaigned hard to try to preserve Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his second term. Leo’s vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times, which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk’s office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3. The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17. It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope's older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal. Prevost's past votes have gone Democratic and Republican Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections. The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections. While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016. The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022. Clashes with Trump Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from President Donald Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants. Earlier this year, Trump called Leo “weak” and captive to the “radical left.” Responding to Trump’s public rebuke, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria in April: “I’m not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for.” “I will continue to speak out strongly against war, seeking to promote peace, promoting dialogue and multilateralism among states to find solutions to problems,” he said. The public dispute has subsided in recent months. A pope who follows U.S. politics closely Leo has made clear on several occasions that he follows local and national U.S. politics closely, and is not afraid to intervene. He has repeatedly called for reflection and humane treatment for immigrants in his native U.S. amid the Trump administration crackdown and mass deportation program. Recently, Leo reiterated official church teaching declaring the death penalty “inadmissible.” He made the pronouncement in a social media post on the World Day Against the Death Penalty, which came as the U.S. announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad . The plans were later scrapped. In 2025, Leo intervened in a debate over abortion, after Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich announced plans to give a lifetime achievement award to Sen. Durbin. The plans drew objection from some conservative U.S. bishops given the powerful Democratic senator’s support for abortion rights. Leo called for respect for both sides, but he also pointed out the contradiction between people who call themselves “pro-life” but also support the death penalty. Also in 2025, Leo said he was “very disappointed” that his home state of Illinois approved a law allowing medically assisted dying, which is condemned by the Catholic Church. ___ AP editor Holly Meyer contributed from Nashville, Tenn. item.title: Pentagon reportedly tells NATO allies to tone down rhetoric about Russia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said. Among the nations that have received ‌messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, ‌which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments. The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The ​latest push has blended incentives for Russia - including sanctions relief - with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations." Among the comments that have drawn US officials' attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said. ‌Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved. None of the people, ⁠who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner. EUROPE SHOULD AVOID "POKING" RUSSIA The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia. Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play ⁠into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine. Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent. Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign. One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a ​Baltic ​official recently that there should be no "poking" directed at the Russians. The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting ​that Russia was "cornered like a rat" as an example of unhelpful rhetoric. It was ‌not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a "rat in a corner" in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine. "We are helping you. The Americans are there," said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon's recent private messaging. "Just don't be loud. Don't make noise." In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be "measured" in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement. The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment. MOSCOW TESTS EUROPE'S RESOLVE One of the European officials said that the Pentagon's advice, ‌while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down ​the probability of Russia testing NATO's mutual defense provisions. Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could ​dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future. The Pentagon messages to NATO officials ​come at a fraught time for European security. Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said. On Wednesday, German prosecutors ‌said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a ​building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg ​area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied. At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration's push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin's continued ​economic isolation. Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington's force posture in Europe, a ‌process that could see a sharp drawdown in America's troop presence on the continent. US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, ​particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia. (Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski in New York, Gram Slattery in Washington and Andrius ​Sytas in Vilnius; Additional reporting by Phil Stewart in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/exclusive-pentagon-tells-europeans-cool-050400616.html

item.title: DOJ subpoenas California election officials in ballooning voter fraud probe
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, stands after holding a Justice Department news conference on Aug. 13, 2026. (Allen J. Schaben/TNS) The Department of Justice has subpoenaed local election officials in at least four California counties, the latest development in its unprecedented effort to usurp the state's authority and prove allegations of widespread voter fraud in the runup to the midterm election. The Chronicle obtained subpoenas sent to election officials in Los Angeles and Orange counties seeking possible instances of noncitizen voting and unredacted information about certain voters, including their registration, address, voting history and citizenship status. Santa Clara County confirmed it had also received subpoenas and inewsource reported that San Diego County officials received them as well. The subpoenas were sent as part of criminal investigations into alleged fraudulent voting by noncitizens. For more election coverage from the San Francisco Chronicle One of the subpoenas was received as recently as Oct. 29. Others were sent in September. The subpoenas reviewed by the Chronicle were sent before a federal judge in a separate case gave a stern warning to First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who has spearheaded the agency's attempts to force California to surrender its authority to administer its own elections, to stop threatening local election officials. At a hearing on Tuesday, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter told Essayli: "This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately." He repeated the message in a ruling Wednesday denying Essayli's attempt to force California to sequester 20,000 ballots the DOJ has said could have been sent to noncitizens. "The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop," Carter wrote. The subpoenas do not mean that the election officials who received them are themselves under investigation. But the DOJ has separately threatened many of the same officials by giving them 48 hours to review lists of alleged noncitizen voters, and threatening them with criminal prosecution if they do not comply. Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan said Carter's warning was timely, and important. His office was at the center of the Trump administration's unsuccessful effort to sequester 20,000 ballots. "Judge Carter's admonishment about threats directed at election officials on Tuesday was well placed and appreciated," he said in a statement. "At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law. Clear court rulings at both the U.S. District Court level and the Court of Appeals have confirmed that. Threats and intimidation have no place in elections. We will take whatever steps necessary to ensure the safety of our employees and to remain focused on serving the voters of Los Angeles County so they can exercise their voting franchise." His office received three federal grand jury subpoenas last week from Essayli and agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the unit the Trump administration has tasked with leading criminal investigations into suspected voter fraud. The subpoenas ask individual election officials to turn over any information that "tends to indicate an alien has voted in a federal election" and that indicates "someone has aided and/or abetted an alien voting in a federal election." The subpoenas also cast a wide net for any communications regarding the back-and-forth between the Justice Department and California secretary of state's office about the administration's downgraded claims of fraud in the state. After initially claiming more than 190,000 noncitizens were potentially registered in California, the federal government went silent for three months before claiming that 20,000 were improperly registered. Federal prosecutors then charged only 28 California residents with citizen-related voter fraud, five of whom are not accused of voting. The subpoenas also seek the registrar's office's methods for preventing voting by noncitizens. The most recent subpoena to Orange County, sent Oct. 23 and received Thursday, according to a date stamp, asks for the unredacted voter records for some 60 individuals from January 2017 through the present. In L.A. County, officials were directed to appear with the requested materials at the federal courthouse in Santa Ana on Nov. 4, one day after the election. In Orange County, the appearance date is Nov. 18. In total, Orange County has been hit with four subpoenas requesting unredacted voter registration information for a total of 80 possible registrants, though Registrar Bob Page noted there has been overlap in the names the federal government has provided. The county also received three subpoenas in September requesting unredacted voter registration material. Page said his office had complied with them. "The Registrar of Voters provided responsive documents requested in the three September subpoenas," he said in an email. "We plan to provide responsive documents for the subpoena delivered to us today." A spokesperson for Santa Clara County said its registrar of voters received two federal subpoenas in September, but did not immediately provide copies. Carter said in his Wednesday ruling that taken together, the DOJ's actions in California represent "a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials." Election law experts quickly condemned news of the subpoenas. "These efforts must be called what they are: a blatant attempt by a politicized and weaponized Justice Department to serve a desperate president's political agenda," Center for Election Innovation and Research Executive Director David Becker, a former DOJ attorney, said in a statement. Citing Carter's demand that federal officials cease threatening local election workers, Becker added, "In response, the DOJ has doubled down." This article originally published at DOJ subpoenas California election officials as part of ballooning voter fraud probes . item.title: 2 men named Dan Sullivan are on Alaska's ballot. Now the DOJ is issuing subpoenas.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Justice Department has begun issuing a new wave of subpoenas stemming from an ongoing criminal investigation into Alaska's Senate race, including the alleged efforts by Democrats to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, multiple sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News. The subpoenas are targeting several Democratic officials believed to be tied to the effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to appear on Alaska's ballot. Nobody involved in the race has been charged with a crime. The department also amended its civil lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion," adding in details from a New York Times report on alleged efforts by people associated with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign to find candidates who could draw votes away from Sullivan. The new filing calls the situation a "conspiracy to undermine the integrity of the electoral process." Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied any connection to the effort to put Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel S. Sullivan has said in the past he is genuinely interested in running. During a briefing with reporters Thursday, a Justice Department official offered perspective into the department's investigative approach in its criminal probe, saying there had been a "significant increase in activity" surrounding the Alaska race over the previous 24 hours. The Times report was published on Wednesday. The Times' article detailed internal emails and text messages from individuals with knowledge of the alleged recruitment efforts — information the official suggested might significantly expand the government's ability to pursue its criminal investigation, since such communications are historically difficult for investigators to obtain without search warrants or voluntary cooperation from individuals with access to the material. The official also alluded to possible investigative steps, like preservation requests to technology companies, search warrants for electronic communications and grand jury subpoenas seeking documents or testimony from those allegedly involved. Asked what federal crimes could be implicated by an alleged recruitment scheme, the Justice Department official identified two civil rights statutes, 18 U.S.C. Sections 241 and 242, as potential roads for prosecutorial action. Section 241 prohibits conspiracies to interfere with federally protected rights, including voting rights, while section 242 centers on willful deprivation of rights under color of law. The official added that prosecutors might, in a situation like this, examine whether there was a coordinated effort to trick voters into selecting a candidate. The official referenced the federal prosecution of Douglass Mackey, convicted of conspiracy for posting misleading messages online during the 2016 election falsely encouraging Hillary Clinton supporters to vote by text message. That conviction was ultimately overturned by a federal appeals court in 2025. Still, a Justice Department official acknowledged that the agency was not aware of any confirmed instances in which an Alaska voter had mistakenly cast a ballot for the wrong Dan Sullivan. "I think I've not heard of that, but it's hard to tell exactly," the official said when asked whether voters had reported confusion or attempted to correct their ballots. Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy directed a separate state investigation this week , ordering Alaska's Department of Public Safety to examine whether the alleged recruitment effort violated state law and whether criminal or civil action is merited. CBS News has reached out to the Department of Justice, Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for comment. Separate civil lawsuit also expands The criminal investigation is ramping up alongside a separate civil lawsuit filed by the Trump administration last week, seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate election results under certain circumstances if the Republican incumbent loses. That lawsuit addresses the government's concerns that votes intended for Sen. Sullivan could instead go to Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whose candidacy was previously challenged by state election officials but ultimately greenlit by Alaska's Supreme Court . The suit, which argues Sullivan's candidacy violates the National Voter Registration Act, was amended on Thursday to include the Times' reporting. It now includes a second claim for relief, arguing the court needs to intervene under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause in order to allow the government to enforce the law and prevent a "conspiracy." "Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief. It also aligns with common sense," the amended complaint reads. Alaska officials have previously asked a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that election administration is a state responsibility. During Thursday's briefing, before the suit was amended, Justice Department officials largely characterized the civil lawsuit as an effort to preserve the government's ability to challenge an election result if deemed necessary. "I don't see this as much more than a preservation suit," one official offered, arguing that once ballots are counted and separated from envelopes, establishing whether individual voters were confused becomes increasingly challenging. The official also expressed interest in obtaining discovery concerning what Peltola's campaign knew about the alleged recruitment operation, and furthermore, when campaign officials may have learned of it. President Trump has railed against the Alaska ballot situation, calling for Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan to be taken off the ballot. Asked by reporters about the Justice Department's lawsuit, he said last week: "Well, I'm the one that said, 'Do it.'" This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doj-subpoenas-alaska-senate-probe-ballot-sullivan-peltola/

item.title: 'I'm deeply hurt': Christa Pike speaks after surviving lethal injection
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Christa Pike said she is in constant physical and mental pain in a statement released one month after she survived an execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30. "I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," she said in the 460-word statement. "I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured." Pike was sentenced to death for the 1985 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville. Pike was 18 at the time. Her execution was scheduled for 10 a.m. Sept. 30 at Riverbend Maximum Security Prison in Nashville, but a last-minute legal battle delayed the proceedings until the evening. She survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs and was taken to the hospital after 9 p.m. that night. Gov. Bill Lee paused all executions and ordered a third-party review into what went wrong. Lee also announced the resignation of Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada . Pike's execution attempt was the second unsuccessful one this year. Since Oct. 10 , Pike has been back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville, where she has been held for more than 30 years. She continues to receive medical care in the prison's infirmary. "I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," her statement read. "But healing is not the same as being okay. "Since that night, I have been largely isolated in the prison’s medical ward, away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me. That isolation brings its own kind of pain." While all executions are paused in Tennessee for now, it is unclear whether Pike will eventually face execution again. Lee has made no indication that he plans to intervene in Pike's case. "As it relates to a particular individual like Christa Pike and her crime, she is still incarcerated under the laws of the state of Tennessee, and I suspect her sentence will be the same as it was before, unless determined otherwise by the courts," Lee told reporters Oct. 28. He said his job is to carry out the law. "The sentence wasn't carried out in this case, and that's the reason that there's an investigation," he said. His administration is finalizing a decision about who will take the top post at TDOC when Strada leaves later this month. What went wrong during Christa Pike's attempted execution? At around 7:40 p.m. on the day she was supposed to be executed, Pike was administered one deadly dose of pentobarbital, the drug used in Tennessee's lethal injection process. Another dose was given at around 8 p.m., according to the timeline of events given by media witnesses who were present. But after an hour of waiting for Pike to die, the execution attempt was stopped and emergency services were called at 8:40 p.m. In other Tennessee executions by lethal injection, including the only successful attempt this year, condemned inmates have died within minutes of receiving just one round of lethal drugs. The first 911 call, made by someone inside the prison whose identity has been withheld from public records, triggered a 26-minute scramble that delayed medics from going inside the prison. The caller did not follow protocol for calling for help from inside a maximum security prison because the caller did not provide to the dispatcher the code required to verify the call is not a prank or swatting attempt. Pike was driven by ambulance to a Nashville-area hospital, where she was intubated and on a ventilator for multiple days. On Oct. 6, attorneys for Pike said she was awake and speaking for the first time since the execution attempt. She was standing up and walking again on Oct. 8 and was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 10. Attorneys for Pike, one of whom was with her throughout the execution day, said it took more than an hour for the IV team to set the lines, and they used at least seven needles. Afterwards, attorneys said Pike's arms were badly swollen, bruised and blistered, possibly from the execution drug leaking into her arm tissue instead of circulating through her bloodstream. Christa Pike's full statement: 'I am trying to heal' The following is Christa Pike's full statement, released one month after her attempted execution. One month ago on September 30, I walked into the execution chamber at Riverbend men’s prison prepared to die. I had made my peace. I had told the people who loved me, supported me and stood by me through the years I was grateful for them. I had also told the people in the room and who were there to witness my execution that I was leaving them in loving kindness. Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain. There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul. I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured. I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger. But healing is not the same as being okay. Since that night, I have been largely isolated in the prison’s medical ward, away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me. That isolation brings its own kind of pain. I spent 28 years in solitary confinement and much of what I am experiencing today is a repeat of that condition. I am searching for meaning in what happened to me. One thing that has given me strength is the extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world. I am overwhelmed by the kindness and prayers of people I have known for years and complete strangers who have never met me. To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words. It is humbling, and it has touched me more deeply than I can explain. I also want to thank the first responders, doctors, nurses and everyone at the hospital who cared for me. They treated me with compassion, dignity and respect. I will never forget their kindness. I also want to thank my attorneys and everyone who has fought for me, stood beside me and refused to give up on me. I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone. Molly Davis covers growth and development in Nashville and assists with special projects. You can email her with comments, questions and tips at mmdavis@tennessean.com. item.title: Pentagon accuses fired 3-star general of leaking classified information
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Sgt. Timothy Jackson/U.S. Army/Associated Press) Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a Pentagon senior military startegist, admitted disclosing classified information about Iran and Ukraine to journalists, according to an internal investigation report obtained by Axios. The report details contacts between Sylvia and two reporters from different news organizations over roughly a year, including encrypted communications and a meeting at a restaurant in Arlington, Virginia, where he allegedly relayed information from a classified document. War Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Sylvia following an investigation into unauthorized disclosures. A U.S. official told Axios that Sylvia acknowledged the misconduct in a recorded interview after failing four polygraph examinations. Reuters and CBS News cited Pentagon officials who said Sylvia failed three examinations. The allegations also have been disputed by some of Sylvia's colleagues. One told The Washington Post that the general repeatedly denied leaking classified information, although he acknowledged having contact with journalists. Sylvia headed the Joint Staff's Directorate for Strategy, Plans and Policy, known as J5, which helps develop military strategy and advise the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. According to Axios, the investigation traced Sylvia's contacts with reporters to at least June 2025. Some communications reportedly occurred through the encrypted messaging application Signal, while another encounter took place at a Silver Diner in Arlington after a journalist lost access to the Pentagon under tightened press restrictions. During that meeting, Sylvia allegedly used notes taken from a classified report to brief a journalist on U.S. assistance to Ukraine. The investigator's report said the journalist was working on a book and had met with Sylvia twice. The general had not obtained authorization from the Pentagon's public affairs office or arranged for the material to be reviewed before sharing it, according to the report. Investigators also examined deleted Signal communications involving another reporter and discussions concerning Iran. Sylvia reportedly said he had deleted a message without responding and believed he had inadvertently erased the entire conversation. U.S. officials, however, suspected the deletion was deliberate, Axios reported. The investigation also found that Sylvia acknowledged being among 20 officials cited in a news report critical of Pentagon leadership. The report described Sylvia as cooperative during questioning and said he surrendered his personal phone for forensic examination. Questions about Sylvia's removal also prompted an unusual reversal by the Joint Staff, which initially issued a statement thanking him for his 32 years of military service before withdrawing it. A U.S. official told Axios that acting Army Secretary Adam Telle's office had pushed for the favorable statement to limit potential fallout from allegations involving classified information. The Joint Staff subsequently withdrew its remarks after learning more about the circumstances of Sylvia's dismissal. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Thursday that an investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations had prompted personnel action to safeguard sensitive information. He also said the matter, along with others, had been referred to the Justice Department for possible legal action. Sylvia, a decorated combat veteran who previously commanded the Army's 101st Airborne Division, did not respond to requests for comment from Axios and other news organizations. His removal comes as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran. A Pentagon official told The Associated Press that Sylvia was not a central planner of the Iran conflict, saying those responsibilities belonged to U.S. Central Command. The allegations arise during a broader Pentagon effort to identify unauthorized disclosures. item.title: El-Sayed and Stevens to make rare joint appearance as Dems seek unity in Michigan
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will campaign Sunday in Detroit alongside former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens, marking their first public appearance together in months after a week in which lingering divisions spilled into public view. The two will be joined by South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the country's most prominent Black politicians, at a get-out-the-vote event at a Detroit church, according to two people familiar with the plans who were not authorized to discuss them publicly. The event was first reported by The Associated Press. The joint appearance — their first since a Democratic unity breakfast days after the Aug. 4 primary — follows weeks of Democrats struggling to unite behind El-Sayed following his razor-thin victory over Stevens. She received significant support from the Jewish and Black communities, leading to concerns about turnout in the general election. Tensions again spilled into public view Wednesday when Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News that he would vote for Republican Mike Rogers . Hours later, Stevens appeared on CNN to reaffirm that she would be voting for El-Sayed, but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.” She said El-Sayed needs to reach out to people who were part of her coalition and “make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls.” Asked Thursday evening about the upcoming event with Stevens, El-Sayed said “we’re always trying to unify the party” and it hadn’t happened sooner because of their busy schedules. El-Sayed then criticized the reporter for the question, saying “nobody cares” about internal party dynamics when the cost of living is so high. While significant, the joint appearance comes just days before the election El-Sayed and Stevens last appeared together on Aug. 6, two days after the primary. Stevens pledged to support El-Sayed, telling CBS News she would do “whatever he wants me to do” on the campaign trail. But divisions from the contentious primary have persisted. Nearly $60 million was spent on advertising attacking El-Sayed, including $30 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel who represents a district with a large Jewish community in Detroit’s suburbs. The church visit on Sunday is intended to further that elusive unity, although its impact is uncertain, given that it comes just two days before the election. Michigan early voting started Oct. 24. “We’ve got a Black and Jewish coalition that came out and voted for me in droves. And I want them to come out and vote for Democrats," Stevens said to CNN on Wednesday. El-Sayed's criticism of Israel, past remarks and his association with controversial streamer Hasan Piker have long drawn concern from some in Michigan's large Jewish community. Turkish and others have said El-Sayed hasn't done enough to address concerns ahead of the general election. The latest controversy centered on an ad by Rebellion PAC, an independent left-wing group, that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. “That has nothing to do with our campaign,” El-Sayed said of the ad. “It’s certainly not what I want to be talking about right now.” Stevens and other Democrats urged him to go further to denounce the content of the advertisement rather than merely distancing himself from it. Trump’s rhetoric and actions create challenges for Republicans. Republicans face political challenges of their own, particularly voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the Iran war and high costs. Rogers has remained closely aligned with the president on most issues, appearing alongside him at a Michigan rally Sunday where he credited Trump with bringing manufacturing jobs back to the state. The rally took place in Port Huron, just across the river from Canada, a country with deep economic ties to Michigan that Trump has targeted with tariffs. El-Sayed has held campaign events in heavily Republican areas, including Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. His team also released an ad featuring clips of prominent conservative figures praising him, including former Fox News host Tucker Carlson, who has faced accusations of antisemitism that he denies. But the ad created another source of friction with some Jewish voters. Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield criticized both the Rebellion PAC ad and El-Sayed’s campaign ad during a call with reporters. “We are one week away from the election, and it feels like the temperature has turned way up,” Starr said. “Instead of things getting better over the last seven weeks, they’ve actually gotten worse.” Rogers, meanwhile, appeared Wednesday with Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas at an event hosted by the Republican Jewish Coalition in Birmingham, Michigan. Cruz called antisemitism “a poison that is ripping the country apart” and accused Democrats of being taken over by “self-proclaimed communists and Islamists.” Trump has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, calling him a “jihadist” and saying Sunday that he was “on the side of terrorists.” Both campaigns make a final push for Black voters Both candidates are trying to win over Black voters, particularly in Detroit's Wayne County, where Stevens defeated El-Sayed in the Democratic primary. El-Sayed's event with Stevens and Clyburn is part of an effort to shore up support among Black voters. Much of El-Sayed's final campaign stretch has included appearances in Detroit. Rogers has also sought to make inroads with Black voters. He visited a reading remediation program at a Detroit high school and discussed housing costs with residents in Pontiac, north of the city. Earlier this month, his wife handed out $10 gift cards at a gas station. The gesture drew criticism from Ruby Farmer, a 68-year-old Detroit retiree. “You’re giving out gas cards in the inner city; you never would come for any other reason,” Farmer said. While Farmer has a bit of difficulty pronouncing El-Sayed's name, she cast her ballot for him three weeks ago anyway. El-Sayed has come out in opposition to policies by Trump — policies Farmer says directly impact her family. “I have a special-needs son,” said Farmer. “He depends on Medicaid. Medicaid has been cut, and for home care workers in Michigan, all the benefits are on hold.” ___ Cappelletti reported from Washington. Mike Householder contributed from Kalamazoo, Michigan. item.title: Netanyahu didn't win Israel's election. He could still come out ahead.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CNN Israel faces weeks, possibly months, of political limbo after final results show there’s no clear winner in its elections . Neither of the two main blocs – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, the other led by the centrist Yashar party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot – have reached the required 61-seat majority to form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament. So how could a new government be formed? Certainly, it does not look easy, with deep-rooted political and ideological divisions making any seemingly straightforward coalition almost impossible. Still, it can be done, even if the result is a tenuous alliance that survives little more than a year or so in office. If party leaders are unable to figure it out in the 12 weeks they will have available, then Israelis will be back at the polls. Here’s some potential scenarios that could avoid that. Scenario 1: An opposition government On paper, the opposition’s surest path to unseat Netanyahu is built on Jewish-Arab cooperation. And that is its biggest obstacle. Two of the opposition bloc’s right-wing party leaders, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, oppose any government that depends on the two Arab parties in parliament – the Joint List and Raam – whether it’s from inside the coalition, or as outside supporters of a minority government. The two leaders have hardened their positions since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023. Only one government in Israel’s history has enjoyed the full participation of an Arab party. Raam was part of an eight-party coalition that succeeded in ousting Netanyahu in 2021, but it collapsed just after a year in office. Even without forming a government, the opposition parties could still work together and leverage their parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker, along with other key positions, and thereby constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government as it continued in power. But the prospects of assembling a coalition to replace him as Israel’s leader remain highly complicated and politically charged. Scenario 2: A national unity government Another option would see the implosion of the two blocs in favor of a unity government. Netanyahu’s Likud party would certainly be involved, along with some of his existing coalition partners, as well as – crucially – at least one party from the opposition bloc. Netanyahu, in this case, is believed to be willing to part ways with his far-right National Security Minister Ben-Gvir – but not from far-right Finance Minister Bezazel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties. Eisenkot , however, has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu, and it would be seen by many Israelis desperate to see the back of ‘Bibi’ as an act of betrayal if he were to change his mind. Scenario 3: A Netanyahu bloc government with defectors Another scenario could see Netanyahu encouraging defections from opposition parties or individual lawmakers. But all four opposition bloc party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and Yair Golan – have declared they will not sit with him. And with Netanyahu’s bloc a full eight seats short, persuading eight individual defectors sets a high bar. Scenario 4: Another election While all these possibilities are being discussed in the background, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will hold a very public round of consultations with the leaders of the parties that have made it into parliament. Once he has solicited their opinions, he will task one of those leaders with the job of trying to form a government. Arab parties are expected to voice their support for Eisenkot, so the Yashar leader could be asked to go first. Whoever gets the nod will have 28 days to complete the job, with a possible 14-day extension if needed. If it all comes to nothing, the president will ask a second leader to have a go. They get 28 days only to sort it out. After that, a majority of Knesset members could ask the president to task a third candidate, who then has 14 days to build a coalition. If none of these produce a breakthrough, there will be another election. The person who appears best-placed to navigate this timetable is Netanyahu. As caretaker prime minister, he can afford to wait: If main rival Eisenkot gets the first shot – and fails – the mandate is likely to pass to him. And if he fails as well, the political deadlock seems certain to lead Israel to another round of elections – with Netanyahu remaining caretaker for months, until another government is formed. A repeat election – which would happen no earlier than next spring – is a real possibility, as these results look set to return Israel to a state of political paralysis and what would be the seventh general election in eight years. item.title: Biggest changes in nearly 30 years could be coming to baby formula
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced on Thursday it is proposing a new rule that will update the nutrient requirements for infant formula. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees the FDA, said in a press release that it would be the first major update to infant formula standards in nearly 30 years. Abbott launches new infant formula made with whole milk: What parents need to know The proposed rule would update requirements for vitamin A, vitamin D, iodine and manganese as well as reaffirm existing requirements for chloride, potassium, selenium and sodium, the agencies said. It would also change the units of measure for two nutrients and request public input on possible requirements for ingredients not currently required in infant formula but sometimes added by manufacturers, they noted. The ingredients not currently required include arachidonic acid (ARA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), and L-carnitine. Some studies have suggested they contribute greatly to infant growth, brain development and health. Andrew Harnik/AP Photo, FILE - PHOTO: In this Oct. 14, 2015, file photo, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration campus is shown in Silver Spring, Md. The agency said there will be additional phases looking at the remaining required nutrients, potential new nutrient requirements and carbohydrate sources. The FDA said it will welcome public comment during its phases and, in the future, will issue one final rule to cover all the proposed changes. The FDA also released new data on chemical contaminant testing for infant formula and found that most samples tested had "low or non-detectable levels of chemical contaminants." "Parents deserve confidence in every bottle they feed their baby," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said in a statement, in part. "We will hold infant formula manufacturers to rigorous scientific standards and put babies' health first." Last year, the HHS and FDA announced they would review the nutrition quality of infant formula in the U.S. CDC says 51 infants hospitalized in botulism outbreak amid ByHeart voluntary formula recall The FDA said the review -- part of its "Operation Stork Speed" initiative -- would look at whether current nutrient requirements need to be updated, including whether additional nutrients need to be considered. Under current law, the HHS secretary reviews the table of required nutrients every four years as appropriate. The FDA currently specifies 30 nutrients that must be included in infant formulas. There are minimum amounts for all 30 nutrients and maximum amounts for 10 nutrients, according to the agency. Among the nutrients currently required are protein and fat, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, folic acid, iron, magnesium and zinc. Oscar Wong/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images - PHOTO: Stock photo of an infant receiving formula. Last year, then-FDA commissioner Dr. Marty Makary discussed removing seed oils from infant formulas. Many commercial baby formulas contain seed or vegetable oils due to the essential fatty acids they provide. "Generally, they're believed to be pro-inflammatory," Makary said of seed oils during an interview on "Fox & Friends" in June 2025. "We don't want babies with general body inflammation. Forty percent of our nation's kids have a chronic condition. Many of those are tied to inflammation and insulin resistance." Doctors have previously told ABC News that seed oils are not pro-inflammatory and can help lower glucose levels, improve insulin sensitivity, reduce bad (LDL) cholesterol, reduce triglycerides and increase levels of positive (HDL) cholesterol. ABC News' Katie Kindelan contributed to this report. item.title: Hackers steal record $6.3 billion from Binance in just 20 minutes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, was hit late Thursday by what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history , with $6.3 billion in digital assets affected. Binance has temporarily suspended customer withdrawals. The company and outside investigators are racing to track down the stolen funds. It said in an X post that $3 billion of the total estimated $6.3 billion in affected assets have been "frozen on-chain so far." Customer withdrawals should resume by Sunday, Binance CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post. Binance added it "will cover all losses" from using its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company reserves. "User funds are safe," the exchange said, adding that it temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed. Read more: How to keep your crypto safe The Thursday attack has rattled crypto markets and related stocks. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) tumbled to around $76,600 earlier Friday morning. Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, led by ether ( ETH-USD ), which dropped 4% to around $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also plunged by more than 5%. Crypto-related stocks traded lower mid-morning on Friday. Shares of Circle ( CRCL ), trading platforms Coinbase ( COIN ) and Robinhood ( HOOD ), and digital-asset Treasury giant Strategy ( MSTR ) each shed 8% to 14%. The frozen assets appear to include over $2 billion in stablecoins. Tether, the world's largest stablecoin issuer, "froze more than 1.567B" of its USDT stablecoin in relation to the hack," CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X . The second-largest issuer, Circle, froze another $800 million "in coordination with law enforcement," CEO Jeremy Allaire said. World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency venture co-founded by President Trump and his sons, said it froze $27 million of its stablecoin, USD1, associated with the hack, according to CEO Zack Witkoff. Although full details aren't yet available, the hack is shaping up to be the largest crypto theft in history, far exceeding the previous record set in February 2025, when attackers stole $1.5 billion from the crypto derivatives exchange ByBit. Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack. Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting for nearly all of those funds. The firm estimated that attackers still controlled over $3 billion in crypto that token issuers cannot directly freeze. The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance, at its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests that the incident may have started with a compromised engineer's laptop. The exchange added that it has found no evidence that wallet passwords were leaked. North Korean hackers swiped $2 billion in 2025 , bringing the rogue regime's total haul since 2016 through the end of last year to $6.75 billion, according to data from crypto firm Chainalysis. "This is likely the largest crypto hack on record, but the key distinction is that it does not currently appear to be a solvency event for Binance," Fundstrat head of digital assets Sean Farrell said. "That meaningfully reduces the risk of a negative feedback loop involving withdrawals, forced selling, tighter credit, and broader deleveraging," he added. Follow Ines Ferré on X at @ines_ferre . Follow David Hollerith on X @DsHollers . item.title: Vivek Ramaswamy's ad using Amy Acton's estranged mother has ended its TV run
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Many, including term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican who has endorsed Vivek Ramaswamy, pictured, had called on him to take down the ad. (Jon Cherry / AP) Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, is leaving the state’s airwaves, the Ramaswamy campaign confirmed Thursday. The ad, which debuted last week to wide bipartisan condemnation, is rotating out after completing its intended run, according to the campaign. The campaign has other ads running in the final days of the race. In the now-completed ad campaign, Donna Arthur — the mother whom Acton says she has not seen since her then-stepfather was charged with raping her as a young child nearly 50 years ago — calls her daughter a liar and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. The ad does not address details of the rape case. But critics panned the Ramaswamy campaign’s decision to use Arthur as a character witness and dredge up painful family history. “I’m learning things even about my childhood right now that I did not know,” Acton told reporters Tuesday during a campaign stop in Youngstown. “I think it is despicable. … I’m sure someday I’ll unpack everything that I’m learning here. But I’m just grateful to Ohioans and everyone, really so much support and love that we’ve received.” The Ramaswamy campaign said last week that the ad would be backed by $4 million in airtime. It began as a minutelong spot but was eventually shortened to a 30-second version. Many, including term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine , a Republican who has endorsed Ramaswamy, had called on him to take down the ad. “Vivek Ramaswamy should never have run his despicable ad in the first place, and it’s totally unsurprising that he took it off the air in the most cowardly way possible, without even the hint of an apology to Dr. Acton, her family, or to the people of Ohio,” Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said in a statement Thursday. The Columbus Dispatch first reported that the ad was ending its run. “It ran to completion, and we’ve put up four other ads,” Ramaswamy said at a Thursday campaign stop, according to the newspaper. WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has rescheduled campaign rallies in a pair of critical Midwestern states that he had previously canceled, according to a person familiar with the plans. Trump has already traveled to both states this month to boost GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas and Republican Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who currently serves in the House.
